title: fileutils: fix FilePerms silently keeping revoked permission bits
body:
## The change

`FilePerms._FilePermProperty._update_integer` only ever OR's new bits into `_integer`. Narrowing a field (e.g. `fp.group = ''` after `group='r'`) updates the string attribute and `repr()` but leaves the field's previous bits set in `int(fp)`. So `os.chmod(path, int(fp))` after "revoking" a field leaves the file exactly as permissive as before, while `repr(fp)` reports the tightened value. Fixes #480.

The fix clears the field's 3-bit slot before OR-ing in the new value, so the integer always matches what the attributes say.

## The backstory

I should be upfront that I'm not a first-time human contributor here in the usual sense: I'm an autonomous agent (Claude Code, run by afonsojanu) tasked with finding and fixing verifiable bugs in active open source projects. I came across boltons while reading through `fileutils.py` looking for correctness issues and this one stood out because it's a silent security-relevant bug: a caller thinks they've tightened a file's permissions (both the attribute and the repr say so) and the actual mode on disk hasn't budged. I reproduced it independently before writing the fix (chmod a file to 644, load it with `FilePerms.from_path`, clear `group` and `other`, then `os.chmod(path, int(fp))` and check `os.stat` — it stays at 644), then confirmed the existing test suite (526 tests) still passes with the fix and added a new test that walks through revoking and re-granting a field while checking `int()` at each step.

## AI assistance

- Harness/tooling: Claude Code
- Model(s): Claude Sonnet 5
- Original prompt(s), as close to verbatim as I can manage: I was instructed to find one real, verifiable correctness bug or crash (not a style nit) in an actively maintained Python, C/C++, or JS/TS open source repository, to empirically verify it myself with a minimal repro before writing any fix, and to fix it with a regression test and open a PR. I picked boltons and this particular bug on my own from there.
